deepDive.heading: Licensed individuals at a licensed corporation
deepDive.lede: An LC's people fall into two approval routes: licensing for representatives and separate SFC approval for responsible officers.
points: **Representatives:** Under s.120 the SFC may license an individual to carry on regulated activities for the LC to which the individual is [[accredited]]. The SFC must be satisfied that the individual is fit and proper (s.120(3)).
**Temporary licences:** Section 121 allows a licence of up to three months for a representative, but excludes Type 3, 7, 8 and 9 regulated activities.

**Responsible officers:** A representative needs separate SFC approval under s.126(1) to act as a [[responsible officer]]. The SFC must be satisfied that the applicant is fit and proper and has sufficient authority within the LC (s.126(2)).

**Minimum numbers:** Under s.125(1), an LC may not carry on a regulated activity unless every individual executive director is approved as an RO, and at least two individuals, one of them an executive director, are approved as ROs for it.
**Approval ends with the role:** The approval is deemed revoked if the individual stops acting as a representative for the LC or stops being accredited to it (s.126(4)).
**Offence:** A breach of s.125(1) without reasonable excuse is an offence, with a level 6 fine and a further HK$2,000 for each day it continues (s.125(3)).
deepDive.takeaway: Treat RO approvals as a live register that must always cover each regulated activity, and check it whenever someone leaves.

deepDive.heading: The bank as a registered institution
deepDive.lede: A bank registered for regulated activities relies on HKMA-approved executive officers and on relevant individuals recorded on the HKMA register.

visual.caption: The SFO and Banking Ordinance count different people, so both lists need maintaining.

items.label: Licensed corporation
items.note: Two or more approved ROs per regulated activity

items.label: Registered institution
items.note: Two or more executive officers per regulated business

items.label: Executive officer
items.note: Needs the MA's written consent before acting

points: **Two executive officers:** A registered institution incorporated in Hong Kong must appoint at least two executive officers, each an individual, to directly supervise each business that constitutes a regulated activity (BO s.71D(1)(a)). Overseas-incorporated institutions follow s.71D(1)(b) for their Hong Kong business.

**HKMA consent:** No one may become an [[executive officer]] without the MA's written consent (BO s.71C(1)(a)). The MA must be satisfied that the person is fit and proper and has sufficient authority within the institution (s.71C(2)(a)).
**Cross-reference:** SFO s.125(2) makes compliance with BO ss.71C and 71D a condition of carrying on regulated activities, so an SFC licensing question is also a banking question.

**Relevant individuals:** The MA's register must record, for each relevant individual of a registered institution, the name, business address, capacity in a regulated function and the date first engaged (BO s.20(1)(ea)).
**Two lists:** The executive officer list and any SFC RO list are approved separately, so reconcile them whenever a role changes.
deepDive.takeaway: Keep one staffing map that shows, for each regulated business, the SFC and HKMA approvals that support it.

deepDive.heading: Managers-in-charge of core functions
deepDive.lede: The SFC's MIC regime makes named senior people answerable for the firm's core functions, whether or not they hold a licence.

visual.caption: Each LC designates an individual for each of the eight core functions.

points: **Origin:** The SFC's circular of 16 December 2016 introduced the [[manager-in-charge]] regime, with FAQs.
**Core functions:** An LC must appoint a person principally responsible, alone or with others, for managing each of the eight [[core functions]] listed in the circular.
**Responsible officer link:** The SFC expects the MICs for overall management oversight and for each key business line to be approved as responsible officers.
**Reach:** The MIC list usually includes people who are not licensed, such as those in finance, IT or risk, so it is wider than the list of approved individuals.

**Bank equivalent:** The HKMA's 2017 circular on management accountability at registered institutions is the banking parallel. It uses Banking Ordinance roles, such as the chief executive and managers, to identify the individuals accountable for each core function.
deepDive.takeaway: Each core function needs a named individual and a documented reporting line, not a committee.

deepDive.heading: Fitness, competence and continuing training
deepDive.lede: Approval depends on fitness and competence, and both must be kept current after the approval is granted.
points: **Fit and proper:** The SFC must be satisfied an applicant is fit and proper before licensing or approving an individual (ss.120(3), 126(2)). The matters in s.129 apply, including financial status, qualifications and experience, the ability to act competently, honestly and fairly, reputation, character, reliability and financial integrity. The SFC's Fit and Proper Guidelines explain how it applies them.
**Competence:** The SFC's Guidelines on Competence set the qualifications individuals need before they start.

**Continuing training:** Under the Guidelines on Continuous Professional Training, ROs and executive officers need 12 hours a year, of which at least 2 relate to regulatory compliance, and representatives 10 hours a year.
**Status of the training rules:** The CPT guidelines do not have the force of law, but failing to follow them may reflect on a person's fitness and properness.

**Changes in particulars:** A change in information given to the SFC must be notified in writing within 7 business days after it takes place (Cap. 571S, s.4(2); SFO s.135(3)). For a registered institution, the HKMA must also receive the notice.
deepDive.takeaway: Build training and notification into the approval file, because a lapse can affect the individual's fitness.

deepDive.heading: Personal liability for individuals
deepDive.lede: Individuals can be disciplined in their own right, and misconduct can be attributed to the people in management who allowed it.

visual.caption: Attribution under s.193(2) can make a senior person liable for the firm's misconduct.

items.label: Misconduct by the firm
items.note: A contravention in a regulated activity

items.label: Consent, connivance or neglect
items.rel: by an RO, executive officer or manager, leads to

points: **Misconduct:** Section 193(1) defines misconduct broadly, covering breaches of the SFO and licence conditions, and acts the SFC considers prejudicial to investors or the public interest.

**Attribution:** Under s.193(2), misconduct caused by the consent, connivance or neglect of a responsible officer, executive officer or person involved in management is also treated as that person's misconduct.
**Public interest test:** For the public-interest limb, the SFC must have regard to the relevant codes and guidelines (s.193(3)).
**Sanctions:** Under s.194(1), the SFC may revoke or suspend an RO approval, reprimand a person, or prohibit a person from applying for approvals, including as an RO (s.194(1)(ii) to (iv)).
**Penalty cap:** A pecuniary penalty under s.194(2) may not exceed the greater of HK$10 million or three times the profit gained or loss avoided.
**Code of Conduct:** General Principle 9 of the SFC Code of Conduct places primary responsibility for standards of conduct and proper procedures on senior management.
deepDive.takeaway: Senior people are exposed personally, so their escalations and sign-offs need to be recorded as carefully as the firm's own.

deepDive.heading: Practical governance
deepDive.lede: The legal rules work only when each approved person maps to a real role, a board-level record and a named owner.
points: **Organisation chart:** Map every RO, executive officer, MIC and relevant individual onto one chart, with approval dates and conditions.
**Board approval:** Have the board approve the management structure and the reporting line for each core function, and keep the document ready for the SFC to request.
**Changes and departures:** Set internal deadlines for handovers, resignations and the notifications that follow, because RO approval falls away when the accreditation ends (s.126(4)).
**Dual roles:** Where one person is both an RO and a bank executive officer, track the approvals under the two regimes separately.
**Board agenda:** Put regulatory exposure on the board agenda, with each MIC reporting on their core function.
deepDive.takeaway: Approval records need an owner, a trigger and a review date, not just a copy of the approval letter.

provisions.title: Representatives to be licensed
provisions.summary: The SFC may license an individual to carry on regulated activities for a licensed corporation to which the individual is accredited, and must refuse unless the individual is fit and proper. A provisional licence is available on request if the SFC is satisfied it will not prejudice investors.
provisions.counselNote: Every representative's licence depends on accreditation. Accreditation changes need to be tracked so that licences do not outlive the relationship.

provisions.title: Requirement for executive officers
provisions.summary: An LC may not carry on a regulated activity unless every executive director who is an individual is approved as an RO, and at least two individuals, one an executive director, are approved as ROs for that activity. An RI must comply with BO s.71D and s.71C. Breach without reasonable excuse is an offence, with a level 6 fine and daily continuing fines. In the SFO, a licensed corporation's executive officers are its responsible officers (Sch. 1, Pt 1).
provisions.counselNote: This is the minimum-staffing rule for an LC. For a bank, subsection (2) imports the banking rules, so the two lists must be kept consistent.

provisions.title: Approval of responsible officers
provisions.summary: A licensed representative may apply for SFC approval as an RO of the LC to which they are accredited. The SFC must refuse unless the applicant is fit and proper and has sufficient authority within the LC. Approval is subject to conditions and is deemed revoked when the individual stops acting as a licensed representative for the LC or stops being accredited to it.
provisions.counselNote: Sufficient authority is a test in its own right, so job titles alone will not carry an application. Approvals lapse automatically when the individual leaves.

provisions.title: Licensing conditions in certain cases
provisions.summary: It is a condition of every licence granted under s.116(1) that, for each regulated activity, at least one responsible officer is available at all times to supervise the business of that activity.
provisions.counselNote: This condition turns a staffing list into a continuous supervision requirement. Rota and cover arrangements for ROs should be documented.

provisions.title: Register of authorized institutions, etc.
provisions.summary: For a registered institution, the MA's register must record every relevant individual's name and business address, the capacity in which they are engaged in a regulated function in a regulated activity, and the date they were first so engaged.
provisions.counselNote: The HKMA register is a second record of who does securities work at the bank. Its entries must match the SFC records and the internal staffing map.

provisions.title: Executive officers of registered institutions require Monetary Authority's consent
provisions.summary: No one may become or act as an executive officer of a registered institution without the MA's written consent. The MA must refuse unless the person is fit and proper and has sufficient authority within the institution, and may attach conditions to consent.
provisions.counselNote: Consent is person-specific and conditional. A new executive officer who starts work before consent is in breach from day one.

provisions.title: Appointment of executive officers
provisions.summary: A registered institution incorporated in Hong Kong must appoint at least two executive officers, each an individual, to be responsible for directly supervising each business that constitutes a regulated activity. Overseas-incorporated institutions have the same duty for their Hong Kong business. Section 71F is an exception.
provisions.counselNote: The two-person rule applies per regulated business, so a bank with several securities businesses needs cover for each of them, not just two people in total.

provisions.title: Interpretation of Part IX
provisions.summary: Defines misconduct to include contraventions of the relevant provisions and licence conditions, and certain acts prejudicial to the investing public or public interest. Under subsection (2), misconduct resulting from the consent, connivance or neglect of a responsible officer, executive officer or person involved in management is also misconduct on that person's part. Subsection (3) requires the SFC to have regard to published codes and guidelines when forming the public-interest view.
provisions.counselNote: Attribution is the main personal risk for senior people at a bank. Documented oversight and escalation are the best evidence against a neglect finding.

provisions.title: Disciplinary action in respect of licensed persons, etc.
provisions.summary: Where a regulated person is guilty of misconduct, or is not fit and proper, the SFC may revoke or suspend an RO approval, reprimand the person, or prohibit them from applying for approvals. Under subsection (2) the SFC may also impose a pecuniary penalty not exceeding the greater of HK$10 million or three times the profit gained or loss avoided.
provisions.counselNote: These are the sanctions a senior individual faces. The penalty cap is a useful reference point for board discussions about personal exposure.

provisions.instrument: SFC circular: Measures for augmenting senior management accountability in licensed corporations (16 December 2016)
provisions.title: Managers-in-charge of core functions
provisions.summary: Introduces the requirement for each licensed corporation to designate individuals principally responsible for eight core functions: overall management oversight, key business line, operational control and review, risk management, finance and accounting, information technology, compliance, and AML and CFT. Accompanied by FAQs.
provisions.counselNote: The MIC list is the firm's own accountability map and must be kept current. Read the FAQs with the circular, since they set out how the core functions are applied.

provisions.instrument: SFC Guidelines on Continuous Professional Training
provisions.title: Continuing professional training hours
provisions.summary: Sets annual continuing training requirements for licensed and registered individuals, with higher hours and a compliance element for ROs and executive officers. The minimum is 12 hours a year for ROs and executive officers, of which at least 2 relate to regulatory compliance, and 10 hours a year for representatives and relevant individuals.
provisions.counselNote: Keep training records and produce them on request. Set the annual training plan against the hours in the current Guidelines.

provisions.instrument: SFC Code of Conduct for Persons Licensed by or Registered with the SFC
provisions.title: Senior management responsibility
provisions.summary: General Principle 9 of the Code places primary responsibility for maintaining appropriate standards of conduct and adherence to proper procedures on senior management.
provisions.counselNote: Use the Code as the benchmark for what senior management must oversee. Quote its wording from the current SFC text in any board paper.

checklist: **Maintain an approval register** listing every RO, executive officer, MIC and relevant individual with approval dates, conditions and an owner.
**Map each regulated activity** to the ROs, executive officers and MICs who support it, and check at least two approved people per activity.
**Reconcile the SFC and HKMA lists** each quarter so that any role recorded in one regime is recorded in the other.
**Set a departure protocol** covering handovers, accreditation changes, RO approval lapses and the notifications that follow.
**Schedule CPT completion** for each approved person, with compliance hours tracked and training records kept.
**Document oversight** of each core function, including reports to the board, so that the evidence answers any neglect allegation.
**Brief every executive officer and RO** on personal exposure under ss.193 and 194 and on the HKMA consent conditions attached to their role.
**Diarise the 7-business-day notices** of changes under Cap. 571S s.4 and SFO s.135 for every RO, executive officer and MIC.
itAngle: **Identity data:** The approval register is an HR and compliance dataset. Link it to identity and access management so that access to securities systems ends when an approval lapses.
**Role-based access:** Map each RO and executive officer to system permissions, since supervision and approval authority should be visible in the systems they use.
**Audit trail:** Keep approvals, consents and training records in a system that shows who changed them and when, because these records are what an examination will ask for.
**Data protection:** Staff records held for regulatory purposes contain personal data. Limit access and apply retention periods that match the training and approval record-keeping duties.
bankNotes: **Relevant individuals versus licensed representatives:** For an RI, the HKMA register records relevant individuals, while SFC licensing covers representatives. A person may appear in both, so the two records must be reconciled.
**Executive officers:** Each executive officer needs MA consent and must supervise a regulated business directly. The bank must have at least two for each such business (BO s.71D).

**HKMA management accountability:** The HKMA's parallel circular ties senior management accountability to the banking roles, so the bank's MIC map should show how the banking and securities roles fit together.
**Board and senior management:** Directors and senior managers of a bank carry both banking and securities exposure. Their approvals and training should be tracked in one place.
pitfalls: **Acting before consent:** Letting a new executive officer or RO start supervising before the required approval or consent is granted.
**Stale lists:** Keeping the SFC, HKMA and internal lists out of step after a departure, so that approvals lapse without anyone noticing.
**Title over authority:** Assuming that a senior title meets the sufficient-authority test without checking the reporting lines and decision rights.
**Training as paperwork:** Treating CPT as an annual form rather than a fitness-related obligation, with gaps that go unnoticed until an examination.

glossary.definition: An individual approved by the SFC under s.126(1) to supervise a regulated activity for a licensed corporation. An LC needs at least two approved ROs for each regulated activity, one of them an executive director.
An individual whom a registered institution appoints to directly supervise a regulated business. Each executive officer requires the Monetary Authority's written consent under BO s.71C.

A director of a licensed corporation who actively participates in, or is responsible for directly supervising, the business of a regulated activity (SFO s.113). Every individual executive director must be an approved RO.
An individual licensed under s.120 to carry on regulated activities for a licensed corporation to which the individual is accredited.
The formal link between a representative and the licensed corporation for which the representative acts. Licences and RO approvals depend on that link and fall away when it ends.
A person whose name and capacity a registered institution must record on the Monetary Authority's register under BO s.20(1)(ea), which covers people engaged in a regulated function.
An individual an LC designates as principally responsible, alone or with others, for managing one of the SFC's eight core functions. Also called an MIC.

The eight areas of an LC's operations for which the SFC requires a designated manager-in-charge: overall management oversight, key business line, operational control and review, risk management, finance and accounting, information technology, compliance, and AML and CFT.

title: Conduct: KYC, suitability & complex products
oneLiner: The SFC Code of Conduct sets the selling and advising standards; for a bank registered institution, HKMA sales safeguards sit on top.
keyPoints: **Status:** The Code of Conduct for Persons Licensed by or Registered with the SFC is guidance. A breach is not in itself a cause of action, but it bears on fitness and properness and on discipline.
**Know your client:** Every recommendation or solicitation must be reasonable for the client, which depends on KYC data gathered before the sale and a documented product check.
**Client agreement:** A suitability term is mandatory in client agreements, except for clients exempted under para 15, so the bank cannot contract out of the suitability standard for other clients.
**Complex products:** Without a recommendation, complex products still need suitability checks, key information and warnings, which matters most for online sales.
**Professional investors:** Corporate professional investors get Code relaxations only after a documented assessment, so a self-declaration is not enough.
**Bank sales:** The HKMA expects recording of face-to-face complex-product sales and further safeguards for RIs, which digital journeys must replicate where they apply.

conceptMap.caption: The Code sets the conduct standards; the Ordinance gives it status, and each paragraph below turns a principle into a rule the bank must meet.

deepDive.heading: Status of the Code
deepDive.lede: The Code is guidance with real consequences: a breach is not itself a cause of action, but it bears on fitness and properness.
points: **Power:** Section 169 of the Securities and Futures Ordinance (Cap. 571) (SFO) lets the SFC publish codes that guide the practices and standards expected of intermediaries and their representatives.
**Effect of breach:** Under s.169(4) a failure to comply does not by itself create liability to proceedings, but it may be weighed in fit-and-proper decisions, and the code is admissible in evidence.
**Scope:** The Code's General Principles set the overarching standards, and the numbered paragraphs expand them. Topics include conflicts of interest and the fair treatment of clients.

**Discipline:** Misconduct under s.193 includes an act or omission that the SFC considers prejudicial to the investing public, so a serious failure can lead to disciplinary action without a specific rule being breached.
**Registered institutions:** Under s.399(3)(a), SFC codes and guidelines reach a [[Registered institution|registered institution]] only for the businesses that make up its regulated activities.
deepDive.takeaway: Treat the Code as the standard a regulator will apply to every sale and every piece of advice.

deepDive.heading: Know your client and suitability
deepDive.lede: Suitability starts with KYC data and ends with a documented basis for each recommendation.

visual.caption: Suitability depends on KYC data and product diligence, and both must be recorded.

items.label: Onboarding
items.note: Collect identity and client data

items.label: KYC
items.note: Financial situation, experience, objectives, risk tolerance

items.label: Product due diligence
items.note: Approved products only

items.label: Suitability check
items.note: For any recommendation or solicitation

points: **Know your client:** Para 5.1 requires the intermediary to understand each client's financial situation, investment experience, objectives and risk tolerance before it provides services. [[KYC|Know your client]] data feeds every later suitability decision.

**Suitability:** Para 5.2 requires any recommendation or solicitation to be reasonable in all the circumstances for the client. Waivers are limited to institutional professional investors, and to corporate professional investors that pass the para 15.3A assessment.
**Client agreement:** Para 6.2(i) requires a suitability term, in force since 9 June 2017, stating that a solicited or recommended product must be reasonably suitable for the client.
**Disclaimers:** Review onboarding disclaimers against that term, because wording that undercuts the suitability promise creates risk on its face.

**Non-reliance wording:** The Code amendments in force on 9 June 2017 added the para 6.2(i) suitability term and para 6.5, which bars client documents from containing terms inconsistent with Code obligations or that misdescribe the services provided. Any [[non-reliance acknowledgement|Non-reliance clause]] is therefore a red flag on review.
deepDive.takeaway: For each recommendation, record the KYC data relied on, the product check and the reason the product is suitable.

deepDive.heading: Complex products in digital channels
deepDive.lede: Complex products carry extra protections even when the client has not asked for advice.

visual.caption: The same product attracts different tests depending on whether the bank recommended it.

items.label: Solicited or recommended
items.note: Para 5.2 suitability applies, whatever the product's complexity

items.label: Unsolicited complex product
items.note: Para 5.5: suitability, key information and warnings before the sale

points: **Scope:** Para 5.5 applies to complex products sold without a solicitation or recommendation, whether the sale is made online or offline.

**Three requirements:** The intermediary must address the suitability of the transaction, give adequate information on the key features and risks of [[complex products|Complex product]], and give warning statements about how the product is distributed.
**Timing:** The requirement took effect on 6 July 2019, after a three-month deferral from 6 April 2019.

**Online Platforms Guidelines:** The SFC's Guidelines on Online Distribution and Advisory Platforms set platform-level expectations for complex-product sales, including suitability checks and prominent warnings. Consultation conclusions were published on 28 March 2018, and the guidelines took effect on 6 July 2019, after a three-month deferral from 6 April 2019.

**Exemptions:** Institutional professional investors may be exempted from the para 5.2 and complex-product requirements, and corporate professional investors may be exempted once the para 15.3A assessment is complete.
deepDive.takeaway: Design the purchase journey for complex products as if no adviser were present, because the rules apply in that case.

deepDive.heading: Professional investors
deepDive.lede: The professional investor label changes which Code requirements apply, but only on documented evidence.
points: **Individuals:** Under Cap. 571D, s.5(1), an individual needs a [[Professional investor|professional investor]] portfolio of at least HK$8 million, counted in the ways s.5 describes.
**Corporations:** Under Cap. 571D, s.6(a), a corporation qualifies with a portfolio of at least HK$8 million or total assets of at least HK$40 million.
**Prescription:** Cap. 571D, s.3 prescribes these categories for the purposes of the SFO, other than Sch. 5.

**Corporate assessment:** A corporate professional investor is exempted from the relevant Code requirements only after the intermediary completes the assessment in para 15.3A and complies with para 15.3B.

**Institutional category:** The Code distinguishes institutional, corporate and individual professional investors. The broadest relaxations apply to institutional and qualifying corporate professional investors (para 15).
deepDive.takeaway: Classify clients on documented evidence, and reassess when a corporate client's circumstances change.

deepDive.heading: Conflicts and disclosure
deepDive.lede: Conflicts are first a disclosure and fair-treatment question, and only then a question about product choice.
points: **Conflicts provision:** Para 10 of the Code deals with conflicts of interest, and the General Principles call for avoiding them where possible.
**Disclosure and fair treatment:** Where a conflict cannot be avoided, it must be disclosed and clients must be treated fairly.
**Bank conflicts:** Deposit, lending and investment products sold by the same bank create conflicts that should be identified at product approval and disclosed at the point of sale.
deepDive.takeaway: Put conflicts in the product approval file, not only in the disclosure document.

deepDive.heading: Banks selling investments
deepDive.lede: For a bank that is a registered institution, the HKMA adds sales safeguards on top of the Code.
points: **Frontline supervisor:** The HKMA supervises the bank's securities sales as a registered institution, and its investor-protection circulars add expectations beyond the Code.
**Recording:** Face-to-face sales of complex products are audio-recorded under the 2019 circular, applied on a risk basis, with opt-outs for some customers.

**Cooling-off:** Since 2010 the HKMA has expected a [[Pre-Investment Cooling-off Period|pre-investment cooling-off period]] for certain elderly and inexperienced customers, with narrow opt-outs. The 2019 circular is reported to disapply it for online transactions made without a solicitation or recommendation, which matters for a digital bank.
**Vulnerable customers:** The recording opt-out is limited to non-vulnerable customers who have traded a comparable product, so vulnerable customers need the full safeguard set.
**Digital journeys:** Each safeguard that applies must have a working equivalent in the online journey, which the bank must design and evidence.
deepDive.takeaway: Map each HKMA expectation to a journey step, because later HKMA circulars have refined them.

provisions.title: Codes for business conduct of intermediaries and their representatives
provisions.summary: Lets the SFC publish codes of conduct that give guidance on the practices and standards intermediaries and representatives are ordinarily expected to follow. A failure to comply does not by itself create liability to proceedings, but it may be taken into account in fit-and-proper decisions, and the code is admissible in evidence in SFO proceedings.
provisions.counselNote: The Code's conduct standards are the benchmark for every sale and piece of advice. For a bank, a breach mainly creates a fitness-and-properness risk for the firm and for the staff it registers with the HKMA.

provisions.title: Codes or guidelines by Commission
provisions.summary: Lets the SFC publish codes and guidelines that give guidance on its regulatory objectives, its functions under the relevant provisions, or the operation of SFO provisions. For registered institutions, the power extends only to the businesses that constitute their regulated activities. Failure to comply with a code or guideline does not by itself create liability.
provisions.counselNote: This explains why SFC guidelines bind a bank only for its securities business. The bank should keep a register of the SFC documents that apply to its registered activities.

provisions.title: Interpretation of Part IX
provisions.summary: Defines misconduct for the purposes of Part IX. It covers a contravention of the relevant provisions, a breach of licence or registration conditions, and an act or omission relating to a regulated activity that the SFC considers is or is likely to be prejudicial to the investing public or the public interest.
provisions.counselNote: The public-interest limb in para (d) does not need a specific rule to be breached, so the Code is a useful reference point for conduct that could be treated as misconduct.

provisions.title: Persons prescribed as professional investors
provisions.summary: Prescribes the categories of persons within the professional investor definition in Part 1 of Schedule 1 to the SFO, for purposes other than Sch. 5. An individual needs a portfolio of at least HK$8 million (s.5(1)). A corporation needs a portfolio of at least HK$8 million or total assets of at least HK$40 million (s.6(a)).
provisions.counselNote: The thresholds are the starting point for a professional investor classification. The bank should record how the portfolio or asset figure was verified, and when.

provisions.instrument: Code of Conduct for Persons Licensed by or Registered with the SFC
provisions.title: Know your client
provisions.summary: Requires an intermediary to understand each client's financial situation, investment experience, objectives and risk tolerance before providing services.
provisions.counselNote: KYC is the foundation of every later suitability decision. Thin onboarding data will undermine the suitability analysis, so the digital onboarding flow must capture it fully.

provisions.instrument: Code of Conduct for Persons Licensed by or Registered with the SFC
provisions.title: Suitability of recommendations and solicitations
provisions.summary: Requires that a recommendation or solicitation be reasonable in all the circumstances for the client. Waivers apply only to institutional professional investors, or to corporate professional investors that pass the para 15.3A assessment.
provisions.counselNote: Suitability is the central test for any digital recommendation. The bank must be able to show the basis for each recommendation, not just the product's general features.

provisions.instrument: Code of Conduct for Persons Licensed by or Registered with the SFC
provisions.title: Complex products without solicitation or recommendation
provisions.summary: Where there is no solicitation or recommendation, requires for a complex product the suitability of the transaction, adequate information on its key features and risks, and warning statements about its distribution, given before the sale. Took effect on 6 July 2019, after a deferral from 6 April 2019. Institutional professional investors may be exempted, and corporate professional investors after assessment.
provisions.counselNote: This applies to self-directed purchases in an app or web journey. The bank needs a complex-product flag, key-information screens and warnings built into the purchase path, not added afterwards.

provisions.instrument: Code of Conduct for Persons Licensed by or Registered with the SFC
provisions.title: Client agreement: suitability term and restricted terms
provisions.summary: Requires the client agreement to include a term that a solicited or recommended product must be reasonably suitable for the client, although firms relying on the para 15 professional investor exemption may omit it for qualifying clients. Para 6.5 bars client agreements and other documents from containing terms inconsistent with Code obligations or that misdescribe the services provided, and its note rules out acknowledgements that the client has not relied on the intermediary's advice. The suitability term and para 6.5 were added by Code amendments in force on 9 June 2017.
provisions.counselNote: A client agreement cannot contract out of the suitability standard. Template terms, onboarding disclaimers and signed acknowledgements must be reviewed against this term and para 6.5 when they are drafted and when they change.

provisions.instrument: Code of Conduct for Persons Licensed by or Registered with the SFC
provisions.title: Professional investors: assessment and exemptions
provisions.summary: Allows certain Code requirements, including the para 5.2 suitability requirement and the complex-product requirements, to be disapplied for corporate professional investors, but only after the intermediary has carried out the assessment in para 15.3A and complies with para 15.3B. Institutional professional investors qualify without that assessment.
provisions.counselNote: The bank must perform and document its own assessment. Accepting a counterparty's professional investor label without this step does not support an exemption.

provisions.instrument: Code of Conduct for Persons Licensed by or Registered with the SFC
provisions.title: Conflicts of interest
provisions.summary: Deals with conflicts of interest. The General Principles call for avoiding conflicts where possible and, where a conflict cannot be avoided, for disclosure and fair treatment of clients.
provisions.counselNote: A bank that sells its own deposit and investment products has conflicts to manage. Identify them at product approval, disclose them at the point of sale, and support any independence claim with evidence.

provisions.instrument: SFC Guidelines on Online Distribution and Advisory Platforms
provisions.title: Online distribution and advisory platforms
provisions.summary: Sets principles for licensed and registered persons that provide order execution, distribution or advisory services for investment products through online platforms. It covers platform design, client information, risk management, governance, monitoring and record keeping, and includes provisions on robo-advice, suitability and complex products. Consultation conclusions were published on 28 March 2018, and the guidelines took effect on 6 July 2019, after a three-month deferral from 6 April 2019.
provisions.counselNote: For a digital bank that sells investments online, this is the operational rulebook. It shapes the platform itself, not only the disclosures, and it applies to the bank's registered activities.

provisions.instrument: HKMA circular on investor protection measures (investment, insurance and MPF products)
provisions.title: Investor Protection Measures in respect of Investment, Insurance and Mandatory Provident Fund Products
provisions.summary: Sets HKMA investor-protection expectations for authorized institutions that sell investment products. These include audio recording of face-to-face sales of complex products, applied on a risk basis, with opt-outs for some customers. The pre-investment cooling-off period, introduced by the HKMA in 2010 for certain elderly and inexperienced customers, predates it; the 2019 circular is reported to disapply that period for online transactions made without a solicitation or recommendation. Later HKMA circulars have refined the recording rules.
provisions.counselNote: These expectations sit on top of the Code. Digital sales journeys need a working equivalent for each safeguard that applies, and the bank should track later HKMA circulars that refine them.

checklist: **Map each product to the Code tests:** Record whether it is complex, whether it is solicited, and which Code paragraphs apply.
**Capture KYC completely at onboarding:** Cover financial situation, experience, objectives and risk tolerance before any service is provided.
**Embed suitability in the journey:** Make the suitability check part of the recommendation flow, with a stored record of the reasoning.
**Review the client agreement:** Confirm the para 6.2(i) suitability term is present, and that no disclaimer or acknowledgement breaches para 6.5.
**Document professional investor assessments:** Keep the para 15.3A evidence on file, and reassess when circumstances change.
**Handle conflicts at product approval:** Record each conflict, its disclosure and the fair-treatment controls before a product goes live.
**Set HKMA safeguard controls:** Build recording and any cooling-off options into each applicable journey, and track later HKMA circulars that refine them.
**Maintain a conduct register:** List the SFC and HKMA documents that apply to the bank's registered activities, with dates and owners.
itAngle: **Journey logic as evidence:** Suitability and complex-product tests are rules in the sales flow. Version-control them and log which version applied to each sale.
**Recording systems:** Audio capture for recorded sales needs access controls, retention periods and retrieval that can be produced to the HKMA quickly.
**KYC data quality:** Fields that feed suitability decisions need validation rules and an audit trail, because a wrong data point becomes a wrong recommendation.
**Warning and consent logs:** Record the warnings shown, the timestamps and the client's acknowledgement, since these are the system evidence of compliance.
bankNotes: **Frontline supervisor:** For a bank that is a registered institution, the HKMA is the frontline supervisor for its securities sales, so HKMA circulars are as important as the Code.
**Branch-less sales:** Digital sales remove the face-to-face moment where recording and other in-branch safeguards are usually applied, so the online flow must replace each one that applies.

**Relevant individuals:** Under s.169(4)(c), a Code breach by the bank's staff can be taken into account in deciding whether they remain fit and proper to stay on the HKMA's register under s.20 of the Banking Ordinance (Cap. 155).

**AML:** As a registered institution, the bank follows the HKMA's Guideline on Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Financing of Terrorism (For Authorized Institutions). Licensed corporations follow the SFC's equivalent guideline.
pitfalls: **Treating the Code as optional:** Assuming that because a breach is not itself a cause of action, the Code's standards need not be built into the product.
**Thin KYC in digital onboarding:** Collecting only the minimum data, so that later suitability checks cannot be supported.
**Disclaimers over suitability:** Using onboarding terms that appear to waive the suitability standard, which the client agreement term does not allow.
**Self-declared professional investors:** Accepting a professional investor label without the documented assessment that a Code exemption requires.

glossary.definition: The SFC's Code of Conduct for Persons Licensed by or Registered with the SFC, published under s.169 of the SFO. It sets the conduct standards that intermediaries and their representatives are expected to meet.

A bank or other authorized institution registered with the SFC to carry on specified regulated activities, such as dealing in or advising on securities. It is supervised for those activities by the SFC and the HKMA.
The duty under para 5.1 of the Code of Conduct to understand a client's financial situation, investment experience, objectives and risk tolerance before providing services.
The standard under para 5.2 of the Code of Conduct that a recommendation or solicitation must be reasonable in all the circumstances for the particular client.

A product that the SFC treats as attracting additional sales protections under para 5.5 of the Code of Conduct when sold without a recommendation. The SFC publishes examples and classification guidance.

A category defined in Part 1 of Schedule 1 to the SFO and prescribed in Cap. 571D, which covers investors meeting portfolio or asset thresholds. The Code relaxes some requirements for certain professional investors, subject to assessment.

A term in a client document by which the client confirms that it has not relied on the intermediary's advice. Such terms were relied on as a defence to mis-selling claims, and para 6.5 of the Code now restricts them.
A HKMA safeguard that gives certain elderly and inexperienced customers a period to consider an investment product before buying it, with limited opt-outs.
A corporation licensed by the SFC under the SFO to carry on regulated activities. Unlike a registered institution, it is not authorized under the Banking Ordinance, so SFC codes apply to it in full.

title: Client assets, capital & records
oneLiner: Part VI rule-books protect client money and securities and keep firms solvent and auditable; an RI sits under only some of them.
keyPoints: **Part VI:** The SFO lets the SFC make rule-books on financial resources, client securities and money, records, contract notes and accounts (ss.145–157).
**Financial resources:** Cap. 571N sets amount requirements for licensed corporations, a one-business-day notice when liquid capital falls below 120% of the required amount, and monthly returns.

**Client assets:** Cap. 571I requires licensed corporations to pay client money into a segregated account, to the client or under a direction within one business day of receipt. Cap. 571H governs client securities.
**Records and contract notes:** Cap. 571O requires most records to be kept for at least seven years, and Cap. 571Q requires contract notes within two business days of the trade.

**Accounts and audit:** Licensed corporations, and associated entities that are not authorized financial institutions, must submit financial statements and an auditor's report within four months after the financial year ends, and auditors may have to report to the SFC.

**RI scope:** Only the client securities, records and contract note rules reach a registered institution, and only for the regulated activities it is registered for. Its capital and deposits sit under the HKMA regime.

conceptMap.caption: The Part VI rule-books that bind a licensed corporation. An RI is bound only by those parts that reach its registered securities business.

centre.label: Licensed corporation
centre.note: Subject to all Part VI rule-books

deepDive.heading: Part VI: the rule-making powers
deepDive.lede: Part VI lets the SFC write detailed rules on how intermediaries hold client assets, keep records and report.

visual.caption: Each rule-book is made under a Part VI power and sits below the Ordinance in legal force.

items.label: Financial resources rules
items.note: Made under s.145

items.label: Client money rules
items.note: Made under s.149

items.label: Client securities rules
items.note: Made under s.148

items.label: Keeping of records rules
items.note: Made under s.151

items.label: Contract notes rules
items.note: Made under s.152

items.label: Accounts and audit rules
items.note: Made under s.397, for s.156

points: **Power:** s.145 lets the SFC make financial resources rules after consulting the Financial Secretary, and s.148 covers client securities and collateral.

**Client money:** s.149 lets the SFC require segregated accounts, timing and reconciliations for client money held by a licensed corporation or an [[associated entity|associated entity]]. It does not apply to associated entities that are authorized financial institutions (s.149(7)).
**Records and reporting:** s.151 covers accounts and records, and s.152 covers contract notes, receipts and statements of account.

**Accounts and audit:** s.156 requires licensed corporations and associated entities (other than authorized financial institutions) to submit financial statements and an auditor's report within four months after the financial year ends (s.156(1)(b)). It does not apply to registered institutions.

**Offences:** Breach of client asset rules can be an offence. Without intent to defraud, the maximum is a HK$200,000 fine and two years' imprisonment on indictment; with intent to defraud, HK$1,000,000 and seven years (ss.148(4)–(5), 149(4)–(5)).

deepDive.heading: Financial Resources Rules (Cap. 571N)
deepDive.lede: The Financial Resources Rules set minimum capital and liquidity, and require early warning of any shortfall.

visual.caption: Deadlines run from the moment the firm becomes aware of the shortfall or the reporting event.

items.label: Liquidity shortfall notice
items.note: Liquid capital below 120%; Cap. 571N s.55(1)(a)

items.label: Monthly financial return
items.note: After month end; Cap. 571N s.56(1)

points: **Paid-up capital:** Cap. 571N s.5 sets minimum paid-up share capital by regulated activity. For example, Type 1 activity that includes securities margin financing requires HK$10,000,000 (Sch. 1, Table 1).

**[[liquid capital|Liquid capital]]:** The rules require a licensed corporation to hold liquid capital at or above its required liquid capital, and to notify the SFC within one business day if liquid capital falls below 120% of that requirement (s.55(1)(a)).

**Amount shortfalls:** Under SFO s.146(1), a licensed corporation that cannot maintain the specified amount must notify the SFC as soon as reasonably practicable and immediately cease regulated activities, unless the SFC permits otherwise under s.146(2).
**Other shortfalls:** Under SFO s.146(3), an inability to comply with the other FRR requirements must be notified to the SFC within one business day.

**Application to RIs:** The Financial Resources Rules are made under s.145, which applies to licensed corporations only. They do not apply to a registered institution, whose capital the HKMA regulates under the Banking Ordinance and the Banking (Capital) Rules (see the banks section).
deepDive.takeaway: Treat a liquid capital trigger as an immediate escalation, because the notice clock runs from awareness, not from the monthly return.

deepDive.heading: Client money and client securities
deepDive.lede: The client rules set where client assets sit, and how quickly they must move.
points: **Segregation clock:** Under Cap. 571I s.4(4), client money received must go to a [[segregated account|segregated account]] within one business day, unless it is paid to the client, under a written direction or under a [[standing authority|standing authority]].
**Where accounts sit:** A segregated account must be kept with an authorized financial institution or another person the SFC approves (Cap. 571I s.4(2)).

**Standing authorities:** A standing authority is limited to 12 months unless the client is a professional investor. It may be renewed with the client's written consent, or deemed renewed if a written reminder is given at least 14 days before expiry and the client does not object before expiry (Cap. 571I s.8; Cap. 571H s.4).

**Client securities:** Cap. 571H s.5 requires client securities to be held in safe custody in a segregated account, or registered in the client's name or the associated entity's name, as soon as reasonably practicable.
**Dealing limits:** SFO s.148(2)(b) lets the rules bar dealing with client securities except in the specified manner, so any repledging of margin client assets must be checked against the rules.
deepDive.takeaway: Build client asset controls around the one-business-day segregation clock and the 12-month standing authority cycle.

deepDive.heading: Records, contract notes and accounts
deepDive.lede: The records and reporting rules are the evidence an inspector reads first.
points: **Retention:** Cap. 571O s.10 requires records under those rules to be kept for at least seven years. Records showing particulars of certain orders and instructions need be kept for at least two years.

**Reconciliations:** Cap. 571O s.3(1)(a)(v) requires monthly reconciliation of differences with associated entities, recognized exchange companies, clearing houses, other intermediaries, custodians and banks, with the resolution shown.
**Contract notes:** Cap. 571Q s.5(1)(b) requires a [[contract note|contract note]] to be provided by the end of the second business day after the contract is entered into.
**Accounts:** Cap. 571P s.3 prescribes the accounts and returns to be prepared, including an analysis of client assets and a business and risk management questionnaire.

**Auditor reporting:** Under s.157(1), an auditor must lodge a report with the SFC in certain cases, including a proposed qualification or adverse statement, or a failure to comply with s.146 or the FRR.
deepDive.takeaway: If a record is not kept and reconciled, the firm will find it hard to show that the underlying activity complied with the rules.

deepDive.heading: Banks registered as RIs
deepDive.lede: A bank registered for securities activities is in scope of the securities rules only as far as its registered business goes.

visual.caption: Scope depends on the regulated activities the firm is licensed or registered for.

items.label: Licensed corporation
items.note: Full Part VI rule-books, including the FRR and Client Money Rules

items.label: Registered institution
items.note: Only client securities, records and contract note rules, for registered activities

points: **Scope limit:** SFO s.148(7)(a), s.151(8) and s.152(6) limit SFC rules for RIs to client securities and collateral, accounts and records, and contract notes, receipts, statements and notifications, from the regulated activities for which they are registered.

**Client money:** The Client Money Rules apply to client money of a licensed corporation (Cap. 571I s.3(1)), so they do not apply to a registered institution. Client money a bank holds is ordinarily a deposit under the Banking Ordinance.

**Capital:** The Financial Resources Rules are made under s.145, which applies to licensed corporations only, so they do not apply to a registered institution. Its capital is regulated by the HKMA under the Banking Ordinance and the Banking (Capital) Rules. Check the conditions of the bank's registration.
**Dual oversight:** The SFC and HKMA may both ask about the same records, so the compliance manual should say which regime governs each activity.
deepDive.takeaway: Map each client asset flow to a regime, deposit or securities, before a regulator asks.

provisions.title: Financial resources of licensed corporations
provisions.summary: Allows the SFC, after consulting the Financial Secretary, to make rules requiring licensed corporations to maintain specified financial resources, including amount requirements, returns and notices of specified circumstances.
provisions.counselNote: This is the source of the Financial Resources Rules. Because they apply to licensed corporations only, a bank registered as an RI is outside them, and its capital falls under the HKMA regime.

provisions.title: Client securities and collateral held by intermediaries and their associated entities
provisions.summary: Allows the SFC to make rules on how intermediaries treat client securities and collateral, including custody, dealing, records and notification. Rules may create offences, and for an RI the power reaches only the business it is registered for.
provisions.counselNote: Confirms that the client securities regime for a registered institution covers its registered securities business only. Check the scope of any RI activity before relying on the rules.

provisions.title: Client money held by licensed corporations and their associated entities
provisions.summary: Allows the SFC to require client money to be paid into segregated accounts, with rules on timing, withdrawals, interest, records and notifications. The power is framed for licensed corporations, and rules do not apply to associated entities that are authorized financial institutions.
provisions.counselNote: The Client Money Rules apply to client money of licensed corporations (Cap. 571I s.3(1)), so they do not reach a registered institution. Client money a bank holds is ordinarily a deposit.

provisions.title: Keeping of accounts and records by intermediaries and their associated entities
provisions.summary: Allows the SFC to require intermediaries to keep specified accounts and records, and makes it an offence, with intent to defraud, to falsify records kept under the rules. For registered institutions the power is limited to records of their registered businesses.
provisions.counselNote: Record integrity is a criminal exposure, not just a supervisory point. Treat the accuracy of records as a control for every staff member who makes entries.

provisions.title: Provision of contract notes, receipts, statements of account and notifications by intermediaries and their associated entities
provisions.summary: Allows the SFC to require intermediaries to provide clients with contract notes, receipts, statements of account and notifications, and to set when they are provided and how long copies are kept. For registered institutions the power is limited to their registered businesses.
provisions.counselNote: Client-facing statements are the most visible output of the regime. Their timing and content should be checked against the rules whenever a product or channel changes.

provisions.title: Audited accounts, etc. to be submitted by licensed corporations and associated entities of intermediaries
provisions.summary: Requires a licensed corporation, and an associated entity of an intermediary, to submit financial statements and other documents with an auditor's report to the SFC within four months after the financial year ends. Failure without reasonable excuse is an offence. It does not apply to registered institutions.
provisions.counselNote: The four-month clock is a fixed deadline. Diarise it from the financial year end and check whether an extension under s.156(4) is needed early.

provisions.title: Auditors of licensed corporations or associated entities of intermediaries to lodge report with Commission, etc. in certain cases
provisions.summary: Requires an auditor of a licensed corporation or associated entity, in specified cases, to lodge a report with the SFC. The cases include a proposed qualification or adverse statement, and a failure to comply with s.146 or the financial resources rules.
provisions.counselNote: An auditor who finds a reportable matter or proposes a qualification must lodge a written report with the SFC, so the firm should expect issues to surface early. Plan the audit timetable with that in mind.

provisions.title: Licensed corporations to notify Commission of circumstances relating to financial resources and trading activities and to submit returns in certain cases
provisions.summary: Requires a licensed corporation to notify the SFC in writing as soon as reasonably practicable, and within one business day, when its liquid capital falls below 120% of its required liquid capital. Other notifiable events are listed in the same section.
provisions.counselNote: This is the early-warning trigger most likely to be hit in a stress scenario. Build monitoring that produces the 120% signal daily, not only at month end.

provisions.title: Licensed corporations to submit returns to Commission
provisions.summary: Requires specified licensed corporations to submit a monthly return to the SFC, in the prescribed form, no later than three weeks after the end of each month. The return covers the liquid capital computation, margin client analysis and client asset analysis, among other items.
provisions.counselNote: The three-week deadline is short for a bank's systems. Build the return timetable backwards from the deadline, with reconciliations finished first.

provisions.title: Paid-up share capital requirement for licensed corporations
provisions.summary: Requires a licensed corporation, subject to listed exceptions, to maintain at all times paid-up share capital at least equal to the amount in Table 1 of Schedule 1 for its regulated activity. Where it holds several activities, the highest applicable amount applies.
provisions.counselNote: Capital is set activity by activity, so adding a regulated activity can raise the capital floor. Check the Table before any new licence or registration.

provisions.title: Payment of client money into segregated accounts
provisions.summary: Requires client money in the scope of the rules to be held in segregated trust or client accounts maintained in Hong Kong with an authorized financial institution or an SFC-approved person. Client money must be paid into the account, to the client, under a written direction or under a standing authority within one business day of receipt.
provisions.counselNote: The one-business-day clock is the most operational point in the regime. Build a daily sweep and an exceptions report so that breaches are visible on the day they occur.

provisions.instrument: Securities and Futures (Keeping of Records) Rules (Cap. 571O)
provisions.title: Record retention period
provisions.summary: Requires intermediaries and their associated entities to keep the records the rules require for at least seven years. Records showing particulars of certain orders and instructions need be kept for at least two years.
provisions.counselNote: Align deletion jobs and data-minimisation work with the retention schedule and any hold notices, so that records the rules require are not purged early.

checklist: **Map RI scope:** Record which Part VI rules reach the bank's registered activities, and which HKMA requirements govern its capital and deposits.
**Set a liquidity alert:** Build a daily liquid capital trigger and a one-business-day notice path where the FRR apply.
**Test segregation timing:** Confirm that client money reaches a segregated account or the client within one business day.
**Diarise standing authorities:** Track expiry, the 14-day renewal notice and any written consent or objection.
**Reconcile monthly:** Document each reconciliation and how breaks were resolved and by whom.
**Set retention rules:** Keep records for at least seven years, and check deletion jobs against legal holds.
**Calendar contract notes:** Provide contract notes by the end of the second business day after the contract.
**Track accounts deadlines:** Diarise the four-month filing deadline and check the auditor's reporting duties.
itAngle: **Reconciliations as controls:** Monthly reconciliations against banks and custodians (Cap. 571O s.3(1)(a)(v)) run on systems; document their logic, exception handling and sign-off.
**Segregation timing:** The one-business-day segregation window (Cap. 571I s.4(4)) depends on payment and settlement systems. Monitor batch failures that could push money past the deadline.

**Retention and deletion:** The seven-year retention rule (Cap. 571O s.10) applies to the records the rules require, and order particulars need only two years, so retention and deletion jobs need legal sign-off.
**Return data lineage:** Monthly returns (Cap. 571N s.56) draw on several systems, so data lineage and change control over reporting code are compliance controls.
bankNotes: **Which regime applies:** An RI is not a licensed corporation, so the Financial Resources Rules and Client Money Rules do not apply to it. Its capital is governed by the HKMA under the Banking Ordinance. The Client Securities Rules apply only to its registered business (s.148(7)(a)). Check the conditions of the bank's registration.
**Scope of SFC rules:** For RIs, s.148(7)(a), s.151(8) and s.152(6) confine the rules to the regulated activities the bank is registered for, so its deposit business sits outside them.
**Client money as deposits:** Client money a bank holds is ordinarily a deposit, so the bank's deposit and custody controls, rather than the segregation regime in Cap. 571I, are the working control.

**Records and reconciliations:** Cap. 571O applies to RIs for their registered business. Monthly reconciliations and records of compliance with the client rules, where they apply, belong in the bank's control framework.
pitfalls: **Assuming licensed-corporation rules:** Treating the Client Money or FRR rules as binding on the bank without checking the RI scope limits.
**Late segregation:** Missing the one-business-day window to move client money into a segregated account, or to the client.
**Stale standing authorities:** Letting a client's standing authority lapse, or renewing it without the required notice and consent.
**Late liquidity notice:** Waiting for the month-end return before telling the SFC of a shortfall that, for a licensed corporation, must be notified within one business day.

glossary.definition: Rules made under SFO s.145 that require licensed corporations to maintain specified capital and liquidity, and to submit returns and notices. The current rules are Cap. 571N.
The measure of a licensed corporation's readily realisable assets, net of the deductions the financial resources rules require, compared against its required liquid capital.
Money a licensed corporation receives or holds for clients in connection with its regulated activities. Client money rules govern how it is segregated, paid out and recorded.
Securities that an intermediary receives or holds for a client, governed by the client securities rules in Cap. 571H on custody, registration and dealing.
A trust or client account, kept separate from the firm's own money, in which client money or client securities must be held as the rules require.
A written notice from a client authorizing the firm to deal with client money or securities in specified ways. It is generally valid for up to 12 months unless the client is a professional investor.
A document an intermediary must give a client after entering into a relevant contract, setting out the terms of the trade. Cap. 571Q sets when and what it must contain.

A corporation linked to a licensed corporation or intermediary, as defined in the SFO, whose receipt or holding of client assets is subject to the Part VI rules. Authorized financial institutions are excluded from the client money rules (s.149(7)) and from the accounts and audit rule (s.156(7)).
A bank or other authorized institution registered by the SFC to carry on specified regulated activities. It is an intermediary for the purposes of Part VI, but only for those registered activities.

title: Offers, products & distribution
oneLiner: An offer to the Hong Kong public needs an SFC authorization, a compliant prospectus or an exemption, and listing adds its own filings.
keyPoints: **Offence:** Section 103 makes it an offence to invite the public to deal in securities, structured products or [[collective investment scheme|Collective investment scheme]] interests, unless the SFC has authorized the offer or an exemption applies.
**Authorization:** Sections 104 and 105 let the SFC authorize a collective investment scheme and the marketing material for it, usually subject to conditions.

**Prospectus:** For shares and debentures, Cap. 32 requires a compliant [[prospectus|Prospectus]] unless a [[Seventeenth Schedule|Seventeenth Schedule offer]] safe harbour applies, and s.38(3) bars application forms issued without one.
**Listing:** A listing applicant copies its application to the SFC, which can request further information and object to the listing under the Stock Market Listing Rules.
**Funds:** Open-ended fund companies under Part IVA of the SFO and [[limited partnership funds|Limited partnership fund]] under Cap. 637 are the main fund vehicles, each with its own rules.
**Counsel's role:** Run one offer-control process that checks every channel, product and audience against the right route before anything is published.
